title: Short Stuff: Evil Eye
summary: Short Stuff episode on the evil eye, a wordless curse or glance believed to cause harm, envy, or misfortune. The hosts discuss its ancient roots (Mesopotamia's Tell Brak eye idols, possibly 5,000 years old), Plutarch's theory that the eyes emit harmful energy, and how it can be unintentional. They cover protective traditions: the Turkish nazar, the Eye of Horus, Indian black dots on infants, ribbons on cribs, amulets, and pregnancy customs such as avoiding baby showers. They also mention a Mediterranean grandmother reading olive oil drops in water to detect the evil eye. Book author Antonio Paglia Rulo, who is Italian and Catholic, is cited as a source. The episode opens and closes with casual banter and a sponsor-free sign-off.

entities.name: The Evil Eye: The History, Mystery and Magic of the Quiet Curse

segments.title: Opening banter and the stink eye
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with jokes about a blown tire and a lost checkbook, then introduce the evil eye, which they call the stink eye, and credit Dave Brus and HowStuffWorks and author Antonio Paglia Rulo.

segments.title: What the evil eye is
segments.summary: Chuck describes the evil eye as a wordless glance or curse, a tradition that goes back a long way, often rooted in jealousy, envy, anger, or greed.

segments.title: Ancient roots and Plutarch's theory
segments.summary: The hosts trace the evil eye to the Greeks and earlier. Plutarch, in his Moralia, described the eyes as emitting harmful energy, which they relate to an ancient theory that we see by beams shot from the eyes. Chuck notes the curse can also be unintentional.

segments.title: Who gets blamed for bad luck
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the evil eye can be blamed for bad things that happen to a person or to their possessions, using exploding smartphones as an example.

segments.title: Pregnancy customs and baby showers
segments.summary: Antonio Paglia Rulo's Italian Catholic background is discussed: baby showers are considered bad luck, and pregnant women wore amulets and said prayers against the evil eye. Josh notes that babies, children, pregnant women, and animals are most vulnerable.

segments.title: Protective talismans around the world
segments.summary: Josh describes the Turkish nazar, a blue eye-shaped amulet given to newborns. Before a break, he sets up the question of its origin.

segments.title: Eye of Horus and the nazar
segments.summary: The hosts discuss protective traditions in India, including black dots on infants, and Jewish ribbons on cribs. Josh links the nazar to the Eye of Horus from ancient Egypt, which was painted on homes and tombs and became simpler over time.

segments.title: Olive oil divination
segments.summary: Chuck describes how Antonio Paglia Rulo's grandmother, a practitioner, dropped olive oil into water and read the shapes to detect the evil eye on family members or neighbors.

segments.title: Tell Brak eye idols and ET
segments.summary: Josh says the evil eye may date back at least 5,000 years to Tell Brak in Mesopotamia, where small eye idols were found. He and Chuck joke that the idols look like ET.

segments.title: Closing remarks and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh suggests saying 'please don't look at me like that' to dispel the evil eye. Chuck closes with the standard iHeartRadio production credit.
